summary: An IAB essay on the end-to-end principle, the core design guideline of the Internet. It traces how the principle has been applied over time and considers how trends such as middleboxes in the network affect it. It then draws conclusions about how the principle and the architecture should evolve.

plainLanguage.summary: The internet works best when the computers at the two ends do the smart work and the network in between just passes things along. This note asks if that is still true.

questions: why do middleboxes break end to end
subtitle: An IAB essay on how the end-to-end principle grew, what pressures it, and why it still matters.

tldr.problem: The end-to-end principle is the Internet's core architectural guideline, but lack of trust, new service models and commercial third parties are pushing services into the network.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB traces how the principle's meaning widened over time, lists the pressures against it, and proposes unbundling it into its consequences: protection of innovation, and reliability and robustness.
tldr.outcome: The document concludes that the principle remains as important as ever, and that any proposal to put services in the network should be weighed against properties such as user choice, service integrity and trust.

facts.label: Two consequences
facts.value: Protection of innovation; reliability and robustness

today: RFC 3724 is an Informational IAB document from March 2004. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it defines no protocol, so it stands as a statement of architectural reasoning.

sections.title: Why Revisit End-to-End
sections.content:
This is an informational essay from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). It starts from the end-to-end principle described in the papers by Saltzer, Reed and Clark. That principle was first framed as a question of where best not to put functions in a communication system.

Over the years it has also come to cover openness, reliability and robustness, user choice, and ease of developing new services. The document looks at how its interpretation changed, at trends that put pressure on it, and at how it might evolve. It builds on the IAB's earlier opinion in RFC 3238 about services placed in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an old rule of thumb for building the Internet. This note looks at how the rule has changed and whether it still works.

sections.title: How the Principle Evolved
sections.content:
The original statement says a function can be completely and correctly implemented only with the knowledge and help of the application at the end points. An incomplete version in the network may still help as a performance enhancement. The example given is delivery guarantees: the ARPANET's "Request for Next Message" never told the sending stack that the receiving stack had properly processed a packet. That is why a reliable transport needs something like TCP's ACK (RFC 793) rather than just an indication that the packet arrived.

Later, RFC 1958 widened the idea to where state lives. Communication state should sit only in the endpoints so that it can be destroyed only when the endpoint itself breaks, which is called fate-sharing. The network may keep self-healing soft state such as routes, while hard state that the application depends on stays at the end nodes.

Mobility is offered as a current example. Mobile IPv6 needs a Home Agent as a routing proxy, but the Foreign Agent of the older Mobile IPv4 design (RFC 3344) is gone, and the end node handles its own care-of address.
sections.plainLanguage: At first the rule was: only the two people talking can be sure the message really got understood. Later it became: keep the important notes with the two people, not with the postman.

sections.title: Trends That Push Against It
sections.content:
The RFC 1958 form of the principle has increasingly been questioned. Earlier IAB documents, RFC 2956 and RFC 2775, worried about NATs and reduced transparency. More recently the concern is services deployed in the network, as in RFC 3238. The text draws on Blumenthal and Clark's point that the Internet began among like-minded, trusting professionals and has very different stakeholders today.

Three pressures are described. Authentication: end users no longer trust each other, so firewalls, VPN tunnel endpoints and certificate servers sit between hosts, although end-to-end mechanisms such as S/MIME can be used instead. New service models: streaming audio and video, and real-time voice and video, treat proper performance as part of the service, unlike email or file transfer. Third parties: commercial ISPs want new services for profit, and corporate and government parties want to interpose in conversations, sometimes to enforce trust and sometimes for reasons such as taxation or censorship.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone knew each other, nobody needed guards on the road. Now that strangers, shops and officials are all involved, many people want to stand in the middle.

sections.title: Applying the Principle Today
sections.content:
The authors reject treating the principle as a fundamentalist rule with no compromise. If the technical community ignores the pressures, they warn, a market opportunity may open for a new community that does not understand the implications of its design choices. Instead they return to what the principle is trying to accomplish, and name two consequences: protection of innovation (changing end nodes or shipping downloadable software is easier than convincing many ISPs to change their networks) and reliability and robustness, which now includes resilience to deliberate attacks.

Because of that, the document argues that trust must become as firm an architectural principle as end-to-end. Before designing a protocol, define the trust relationships between the network elements and draw trust boundaries. Communication across a boundary may need cryptographic or other protection, and a recipient should minimize state before validating a sender's credentials, to avoid a memory depletion denial of service.

For applications, services in the network need not violate the principle if they work with the explicit knowledge and involvement of the endpoints. The result is a distributed application, where the principle applies to each connection. The document also notes that standards have become an arena for conflict, for example ISPs avoiding interdomain QoS because of DoS risk while some users want it (RFC 2990).
sections.plainLanguage: Do not follow the old rule blindly. Ask what it was protecting, which is easy new ideas and things that keep working, and also make sure you know whom you can trust.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
The principle continues to guide Internet standards and remains as important as in the past. Unbundled into its consequences, it often leads to a distributed design where the principle applies between the pieces of an application, while innovation, reliability and robustness apply to the whole application.

The second-order properties it produced are described as at least as important as the principle itself: end user choice and empowerment, integrity of service, support for trust, and "good network citizen behavior". Any proposal to incorporate services in the network should be weighed against these before proceeding.

The security section says the document proposes no new protocols and so has no security considerations in that sense, though the discussion covers privacy and integrity issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule is still a good guide. If someone wants to put a new helper in the middle, first check that it keeps things fair, safe and open for everyone.
